catalog_quote: 2.4.3 Stress. The main stress in Elfdalian usually falls on the first root syllable. This is true for the majority of native words, for example, rakke [ˈrɑ̀kːe] ‘dog’; nammen [ˈnɑ̀mːen] ‘name’; båkå [ˈbɔ̀kɔ] ‘to bake’. There are, however, many exceptions. For instance, many loanwords have non-initial stress: akudira [ɑkʉˈdìːrɑ] ‘to talk’ (< Fr. accorder); kumia [kʉˈmìːɑ] ‘anecdote’ (< Lat. comoedia). However, the tendency is stronger than in Swedish to move the stress to the initial syllable in loanwords: kamrat [ˈkɑ̀mːˌrɑːt] ‘pal, comrade’ (< Fr. camarade, cf. Sw. [kamˈrɑ́ːt]); putell [ˈpʉ̀telː] ‘bottle’ (< Fr. bouteille ...); studir [ˈstʉ̀diːr] ‘to study’ ... Certain foreign suffixes are always stressed, for instance -inna ‘-ess’; -log ‘-logist’; -siuon ‘-tion’. Likewise, a few foreign prefixes are almost never stressed, for example, fe(r)- or bi- (both from Low German via Swedish). .…

tone_statements.quote: The Elfdalian tones or melodious accents, grave and acute, can be roughly described as follows: The grave accent has a falling tone on the first and a rising tone on the second syllable, as in kulla /kʏlːɐ/ ‘girl’, whereas the acute has a rise on the first and a fall on the second syllable, as in fistjin /fɪstsɪn/ ‘the fish’. … One such subtype, the level stress (Swedish jämviktsaccent), is applied to words with two short syllables. The tone on both syllables is high and level, as in fårå /fɔrɔ/ ‘go’

(2) Deciding source is a 2024 open-access UCL Press reference grammar with a dedicated stress section -- the best available description; Glottolog's alternatives are a 599-pp Swedish grammar (2012) that S&L build on, a 1909 morphology/syntax, and older Dalecarlian phonologies of other parishes. sources.citation: Kristoffersen, Gjert. 2010. Fra jamvekt til etterleddstrykk og tonelag 3: Kvantitetsomleggingen i Ovansiljan. Maal og Minne 2010(2): 1-57.
sources.quote: p.7-8: short-syllabicity (kortstavighet) with 'jamvekt' prosody is preserved in Älvdalen (also Skattungbyn/Orsa, Våmhus); Nyström 1991 and Kristoffersen 2007b/2008 show that in Älvdalsmålet the tonal contour of jamvekt words is a shortened accent-2 melody, i.e. jamvekt and ordinary accent 2 are complementary variants of the same unit conditioned by root-syllable weight (so root/initial stress stands). p.36 (sect. 5.3): in Östre Mora (Nusnäs, Garsås; a Moramål variety inside Glottolog's dale1238) old jamvekt words keep a short root syllable while the final syllable has been lengthened 'og har f
sources.note: Fieldwork-based acoustic study of neighbouring Ovansiljan varieties inside the same Glottolog languoid (dale1238 = Dalecarlian): documents final stress in old jamvekt words in Östre Mora (p.36) and summarises the Älvdalen level-stress literature (pp.7-8); supports a within-languoid variation caution.

sources.citation: Levander, Lars. 1925. Dalmålet: beskrivning och historia. I. Uppsala: Appelberg. Chapter 'Accent', pp. 49-54 (page scan from Umeå UB digital collections, digital.ub.umu.se relation/1065027 ff.).
sources.quote: p.49: Levander explicitly sets aside 'frågan om olika stavelsers tryckstyrka i förhållande till varandra (betoning)' and treats the accents (taktformerna). p.50: 'Dalmålet har dessa två accenter [akut, grav] men dessutom också en tredje, som enklast kan kallas jämviktsaccent, och som uppträder i två- eller flerstaviga, kortstaviga ord. I forndalskan -- liksom ännu i Älvdalsmålet -- torde den ha utmärkts av att både tryckstyrka och tonhöjd voro påfallande jämnt fördelade på stavelserna, så att man mången gång kan vara tveksam om, på vilken stavelse huvudtonen ligger.' Also p.50: monosyllables c
sources.note: Classic primary description of Dalecarlian accent and quantity covering all dale1238 varieties; pp.49-54 downloaded and read (level stress in short-root words in Älvdalen); remaining accent/quantity pages available as page scan only.

sources.citation: Fransson, Linnéa & Eva Strangert. 2005. Word accents over time: comparing present-day data with Meyer's accent contours. In Anders Eriksson, Åsa Abelin & Jonas Lindh (eds.), Proceedings FONETIK 2005, 79-82. Göteborg: Department of Linguistics, Göteborg University (open copy: urn:nbn:se:umu:diva-7478).
sources.note: Describes another variety. Two word accents, acute and grave, each one tonal peak differing in timing (grave later, now after the VC boundary); shown for the Leksand, Rättvik and Malung dialects of Dalarna, not Elfdalian.

tone.quote: The typologies differentiate a number of dialect areas by the number and timing of tonal peaks. The typical Dalarna dialects, the focus of the present study, are characterized as one-peak accents, both the acute and grave accent having one peak, but with a later timing of the grave accent peak. … The material consisted of two words produced in isolation, Polen /'po:len/ ‘Poland’ (acute), and pålen /'pò:len/ ‘the pole’ (grave).
